---
title: "Before Lesson 1"
---

Before any theory, you need one reliable path from code to sound. Install Sonic
Pi 5.0.0 from [sonic-pi.net](https://sonic-pi.net/); the download page covers
macOS, Windows, Linux and Raspberry Pi. Treat the version number as part of your
setup, as much as the speakers are. A later release can change a synth default,
and then two people hear different evidence from identical code.

Open Sonic Pi, paste this into an empty buffer, and press **Run**.

```{.ruby audio=""}
play 60
```

One note, and it draws a useful line. Hear it and your program is reaching the
audio output. Hear nothing and the problem is somewhere between Sonic Pi and
your ears, so leave the code alone and check volume, output device, and the log
pane. If you start editing a correct line while diagnosing silence, you'll have
two problems before you've understood the first one.

Headphones, or speakers with some real bass, will help you throughout. Part 1
compares frequencies down around 200 Hz, and Part 10 builds bass lines whose
shape vanishes entirely through small laptop speakers. Keep the level low enough
that repeated drills stay comfortable.

## Why the version is pinned

Every example targets **Sonic Pi 5.0.0**. The extracted Ruby passes syntax
checks, but the manuscript hasn't yet had its full runtime and listening pass.
That's why each lesson is marked `draft` and carries a note at the top, and why
you'll see empty audio attributes where recordings will eventually sit. A syntax
checker reads Ruby grammar. It can't hear a melody or predict what Sonic Pi does
with a call.

Running something else? Open **Help, About**, write the number down, and expect
to adapt. Synth defaults, samples and function behaviour all move between
releases. When an example parses but behaves oddly, the log tells you what the
runtime objected to and the help pane documents the API you actually have
installed. Both beat guessing at the code.

## Three panes worth knowing

Almost everything happens in three places. **Buffers** hold code, and a fresh
one keeps definitions and live loops from the last lesson out of the next.
The **log** prints messages, notes and errors, giving you a second account of
the performance when your ears are uncertain. The **help** pane documents the
synths, samples and functions in your installed version.

On macOS, `Cmd-R` runs the buffer and `Cmd-.` stops everything. On Windows and
Linux, that's `Alt-R` and `Alt-.`. Learn the stop command before you run your
first live loop, not after.

## A first sound

This next program is a preview, not a test. Paste it into a fresh buffer and
listen through two repetitions before you try to understand every line. Parts 0
through 3 will unpack its tempo, synth choice, array, timed playback and
concurrent loops. For now, notice how little data it takes to describe something
that already sounds like music.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

# E minor pentatonic. No note in it can clash with the bass, which keeps this
# first experiment about rhythm and timbre.
melody = [:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :d5, :b4, :a4, :g4]

live_loop :tune do
  melody.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.4
    sleep 0.25
  end
end

live_loop :bass do
  play :e2, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7, cutoff: 70
  sleep 2
end
```

After two repetitions, swap `:pluck` for `:prophet` and run again. Pitches and
timing haven't moved, so the softer attack and longer body belong entirely to
the instrument. Now put `:pluck` back and replace `melody` with
`[:e4, :f4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :c5, :d5, :e5]`. This time the instrument holds still
while the note collection changes. Do those new notes sit differently over the E
in the bass? They do, and Parts 2 and 5 explain why.

Press the stop shortcut before you carry on. Live loops keep running even after
you've moved to another buffer.

## How to work through this draft

Go in order. The representation accumulates, and skipping ahead means meeting a
data model without the reason it exists. The event schema introduced before
harmony comes back in notation, transcription and arrangement, which is what
lets later examples concentrate on music instead of rebuilding their scaffolding
each time.

Most lessons follow a familiar arc: meet the idea, run a complete program,
isolate one change, work out what you heard, then use the idea on something
bigger. The section headings tell you which part you're in.

Use the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd) after a real attempt, not
before. The [glossary](appendix/glossary.qmd) recovers a term, the [Sonic Pi
cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd) recovers a call, and the [sources
ledger](appendix/sources.qmd) covers the provenance you'll need once you start
transcribing.

When a lesson surprises you, write down the version, the exact edit, the log
output, and what you heard. Keep syntax failure separate from Sonic Pi runtime
failure, and keep both separate from a timing problem or a straightforward
disagreement with the prose. That small discipline turns "it didn't work" into
evidence somebody else can follow. It's also exactly what's needed to move a
lesson from `draft` to `tested`.
